newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria oil refinery catches up European standard.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria oil refinery catches up European standard.

text.p: Bulgaria's biggest oil refinery Neftochim said on Wednesday it would switch to a higher quality gasoline from April 1 to get closer to European environmental standards.
Neftochim spokeswoman Tatyana Hadzhieva said the refinery would stop producing 86 and 93 octane leaded gasoline and replace them with 91 octane.

"Under the new structure for petrol production from April 1 the country's petrol stations will sell three types of petrol, 91 octane and 98 octane super and 95 octane unleaded," Hadzhieva told Reuters.

Bulgarians, who before the overthrow of communism in 1989 would queue up to 15 years to buy Russian-made cars, have recently seen their country flooded with second-hand vehicles from Western Europe and new limousines.
Officials said demand for higher octane gasoline was rising. They said demand for unleaded petrol in the country was expected to rise to 80 percent by the year 2000 from the current 23 percent.
But the debt-ridden refinery will need some $100 million to reconstruct its old units.

Bulgaria's interim government said recently it would sell a stake in Neftochim. Russia's state oil holding company Rosneft said earlier this month it was interested in buying a majority stake in the refinery.
Neftochim, which was forced to limit its sales last month due to a lack of cash to buy crude, now refines 15,000 tonnes of crude per day.
The government raised the unrealistically low fuel prices by up to 178 percent last month to ease crippling fuel shortages.
The refinery, which meets almost 100 percent of the country's needs, now sells daily some 1,200 tonnes of petrol from some 3,000 in December due to fuel's high prices, officials said.

Neftochim, which currently has only 30,000 tonnes of crude in stock, expects by the end of the week a second tanker of about 70,000 tonnes of Iraqi crude, which will be supplied from Rosneft's quota under the U.N. approved oil-for-food deal.
